### Bellvitge coordinates in Spain a trail of a self-administered injection that improves myasthenia gravis from the first week onward

  * Improvements in daily activities were observed from the first week, while improvements in muscle strength were seen from the fourth week.
  * The international trial, published in JAMA Neurology, included 260 patients from 113 centres across 20 countries.
  * Bellvitge cares for around 450 people with myasthenia gravis and currently has three active studies on this rare diseases.

Image: Miastenia Bellvitge_NOTI

GO BACK

  * Speaking, chewing, swallowing, walking, or keeping one’s arms raised can become difficult tasks for people living with myasthenia gravis. Muscle weakness typically worsens with repeated movement and often becomes more noticeable as the day progresses. The Bellvitge Universitary Hospital and IDIBELL coordinated Spain’s participation in PREVAIL, an international phase 3 clinical trial evaluating gefurulimab, an experimental treatment for adults with generalized myasthenia gravis who have antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, the most common form of the disease.The trial enrolled 260 patients from 113 centers in 20 countries. International collaboration is particularly important in rare diseases, as it allows researchers to recruit enough participants to generate robust results. Findings published in JAMA Neurology showed that patients receiving the experimental treatment experienced greater improvements than those receiving placebo. Improvements in daily activities began to be observed during the first week, while clinical improvements in muscle strength became evident from the fourth week onward. These benefits were maintained throughout the six-month study period.Dr. Carles Casasnovas, neurologist at the Neuromuscular Diseases Unit of Hospital de Bellvitge and researcher at the Neurometabolic diseases group at IDIBELL and CIBERER, served as the study coordinator in Spain and principal investigator at Bellvitge. Dr. Velina Nedkova and Dr. Moisés Morales also participated as sub-investigators. 

Improvements in muscle strength and daily function

After six months, 46.3% of patients receiving the experimental treatment achieved the muscle-strength improvement threshold defined as a response criterion in the study, compared with 25.2% in the placebo group. In other words, nearly half of treated patients responded, compared with one quarter of those who received placebo.

For daily activities, nearly two-thirds of treated patients (65.5%) achieved the predefined improvement criterion, compared with 52.2% of patients in the placebo group.

“These improvements are important because they can translate into fewer symptoms and greater ability to carry out everyday activities,” explains Dr. Casasnovas.

The incidence of adverse events was similar in both groups. Bellvitge continues to participate in the extension phase of the trial, which will provide additional data on the long-term effects and safety of the treatment.

The treatment is administered as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection that patients or caregivers can give at home. If approved and incorporated into clinical practice, this approach could provide greater autonomy, eliminate the need for regular travel to healthcare facilities, and reduce dependence on hospital day-care units for treatment administration.

 

A rare disease affecting nearly 450 Bellvitge patients

Myasthenia gravis is a chronic autoimmune disease that disrupts communication between nerves and muscles. It causes muscle weakness and fatigue, which worsen with activity and improve with rest. The condition can occur at any age but is more common in women under 40 and men over 60 years of age. It may also cause drooping eyelids, double vision and, in the most severe cases, respiratory difficulties.

According to the Spanish Society of Neurology, more than 16,000 people live with myasthenia gravis in Spain. Although there is currently no cure, available treatments can control symptoms and allow many patients to lead a normal or near-normal life. Research remains essential to expand therapeutic options and better tailor them to individual patient needs.

The Neuromuscular Diseases Unit at Bellvitge cares for approximately 450 people with myasthenia gravis. The unit has participated in four clinical trials on the disease and currently has three ongoing studies. The hospital is a national reference center (CSUR) for rare neuromuscular diseases and is part of both the Catalan and European reference networks.

This research is part of REMMA Bellvitge, IDIBELL’s research program specifically dedicated to rare adult diseases. The program bridges research and clinical care to improve diagnosis and accelerate patient access to new treatments. Participation in international studies such as PREVAIL is one of the keyways to speed up the arrival of new therapeutic alternatives for patients.

The PREVAIL trial was funded by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease, which participated in the study design and development, data analysis, and manuscript preparation.

 

 

 

About Bellvitge University Hospital

Bellvitge University Hospital is a public, university-affiliated, research-driven and innovative hospital. With more than 5,200 highly qualified and committed professionals, it serves as the local hospital for residents of L’Hospitalet de Llobregat and El Prat de Llobregat, while also acting as a highly specialized referral center for two million people across southern Catalonia. It performs more complex surgical procedures than any other hospital in Catalonia, particularly in oncological surgery, and is a member of the Bellvitge Health Campus, recognized by the Organisation of European Cancer Institutes (OECI) as a Comprehensive Cancer Centre for excellence in cancer care, research and education. The hospital integrates patient experience into all its projects and promotes close collaboration with primary care and neighboring hospitals. Focused on personalized medicine, it offers state-of-the-art genetic and imaging diagnostic technologies for cancer and rare diseases, complemented by its High Precision Diagnostic Center, home to the first PET/MRI system in Spain’s public healthcare network. Each year, the hospital performs approximately 26,000 major surgeries, records 39,000 admissions, delivers 400,000 outpatient visits and conducts around 100,000 diagnostic tests.

 

About IDIBELL

The Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL) is a research center established in 2004 and specialized in cancer, neuroscience, translational medicine and regenerative medicine. It brings together more than 1,500 professionals working across 73 research groups and publishes over 1,400 scientific articles annually. IDIBELL is jointly governed by Bellvitge University Hospital, Viladecans Hospital of the Catalan Health Institute, the Catalan Institute of Oncology, the University of Barcelona, and the City Council of L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. The institute is a member of the University of Barcelona International Excellence Campus (HUBc) and part of the CERCA network of research centers supported by the Government of Catalonia. In 2009, it became one of the first five Spanish research centers accredited as a Health Research Institute by the Carlos III Health Institute. IDIBELL also participates in the European Union’s HR Excellence in Research program and is a member of EATRIS and REGIC. Since 2018, it has been an Accredited Centre of the AECC Scientific Foundation (FCAECC).

Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22062)
【turn1054academia21】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
Authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson, Shawntel K. David, Mohammed Sameeruddin, Bernhard Suter, Zhandong Liu, Davut Pehlivan, Hu Chen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:24:47 2026

Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.
